The maximum body length attained by the Red roach (Achondrostoma arcasii) approaches 25 centimeters [Li = 25 centimeters], a value that places this small-bodied leuciscid among the more diminutive members of the Iberian freshwater fish fauna. Field surveys conducted throughout the species' restricted distribution range in northern and central Spain indicate that growth typically proceeds steadily during the first few years of life, with individuals reaching approximately half their ultimate length by the end of the second growing season. This relatively modest final size is thought to be an adaptation to the seasonal and often unpredictable hydrology of the Mediterranean streams the fish inhabits, where smaller body size confers an advantage during periods of low water or elevated metabolic demands. When reared in the laboratory under constant thermal conditions of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the embryonic incubation period lasts a total of 17 days [ab = 17 days] until hatching occurs, after which the yolk-sac larva undergoes a brief endogenous feeding stage before transitioning to active exogenous feeding.

The timing of early life history events in Achondrostoma arcasii is tightly linked to temperature, with development proceeding more rapidly under warmer conditions. Hatching in this species occurs approximately 4 days after fertilisation at a stable temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], and the prolarva then begins absorbing its yolk reserves. The wet weight at birth, measured immediately after chorion rupture, is a mere 0.0009 grams [Wwb = 0.0009 grams], reflecting the small egg diameter that is characteristic of the genus. Newly emerged larvae are transparent, measure only a few millimeters in length, and depend entirely on their endogenous yolk for the first several days of life. The onset of first exogenous feeding typically follows yolk absorption, and under optimal laboratory conditions, this transition occurs without significant mortality. The species' reproductive strategy, producing numerous small offspring, is consistent with a capacity for rapid population recovery following environmental disturbance.

Sexual maturation in female Red roach occurs at a modest body size, with the total length at puberty being approximately 4.4 centimeters [Lp = approximately 4.4 centimeters]. Correspondingly, the wet weight at puberty for females is estimated at 0.76 grams [Wwp = 0.76 grams], which represents only a small fraction of the maximum adult body mass. This early attainment of reproductive capacity is a common life history tactic among small-bodied leuciscids inhabiting unpredictable environments, as it increases the probability that at least some individuals will reproduce before encountering a catastrophic mortality event. The transition involves a complex cascade of physiological changes including activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, which drives vitellogenesis and eventual oocyte maturation. Gravid females can be identified by their distended abdomen during the spawning season, which in the wild typically spans the spring months when water temperatures rise and day length increases. The relatively small size at maturation implies that investment in reproduction begins early, potentially at the cost of reduced individual growth rate thereafter.

The maximum adult body mass recorded for the species, based on measurements of large, reproductively active individuals, is 162 grams [Wwi = 162 grams]. This ultimate wet weight is attained after several years of growth, during which the fish allocates resources toward both somatic development and, once maturity is reached, gonadal production. In the laboratory, the total lifespan observed under constant conditions at 15 °C [T = 15 °C] extends to approximately 14 years [am = approximately 14 years], although field data suggest that few wild individuals survive beyond a decade due to predation, competition, and habitat degradation. The species is iteroparous, meaning individuals spawn repeatedly across multiple breeding seasons once they have reached maturity, and this repeated reproductive effort is a key feature of its life history. Older, larger females are known to produce more eggs per spawning event, contributing disproportionately to the next generation. The long reproductive lifespan helps buffer the population against years of poor recruitment, which are common in the variable streams the Red roach occupies.

Reproductive output in Achondrostoma arcasii is characterised by a maximum reproductive rate of approximately 12 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 12 eggs per day], achieved when females are maintained under optimal conditions at a temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. When expressed over the course of a typical spawning season, this translates into a high fecundity, as each female can produce multiple clutches of eggs, with spawning events occurring every few days. The timing of first reproduction in the wild is connected to the attainment of a threshold body size rather than a fixed age, but under laboratory conditions at 15 °C [T = 15 °C], females are capable of their first breeding event after approximately 365 days [tR = approximately 365 days], reflecting the slow, temperature-dependent pace of gonadal development in this cool-water-adapted species. This delay before first reproduction ensures that individuals have accumulated sufficient energy reserves to support the high metabolic costs of gametogenesis and spawning behaviour. Field observations confirm that spawning is initiated when water temperatures begin to rise in early spring, and the adhesive eggs are deposited over gravel substrates.
